### FAQ

**How much does Google Ads cost in the UK?** There is no fixed price. You set an average daily budget and pay for each click, and the price of a click is set in an auction. In Google's planning data for November 2026, top of page bids for the 42 UK searches in this guide ran from about 20p for running shoes to more than £100 for HR software.

**How much can Google charge me in a month?** Google says you will not pay more than 30.4 times your average daily budget in a month for most campaigns. A budget of £50 a day therefore has a monthly limit of £1,520. For adverts served in the United Kingdom, a 2% UK DST Fee is added on top of that.

**Can Google spend more than my daily budget?** Yes, on a single day. Google's help page says the daily spending limit is two times your average daily budget for most campaigns, and that on other days the campaign may spend less. The monthly limit of 30.4 times the daily budget still applies.

**Why are my clicks more expensive than the Keyword Planner estimate?** The estimate is a range for one phrase across the area you chose. The real price is set in each auction and, in Google's words, depends on your competition, the context of the person's search and your ad quality at that moment. A city, a competitive niche or a weak landing page all raise it.

**Does the cost of Google Ads include VAT?** For a UK billing address, Google Ireland does not add VAT to the invoice, and a VAT registered business accounts for it under the reverse charge. The 2% UK DST Fee is a separate line. Both are explained in the guide to the Google Ads invoice and VAT on this site.

**Is the cost of Google Ads the same as the cost of PPC management?** No. This guide covers what you pay Google for clicks. A fee paid to an agency or a consultant to run the account is a separate cost and is invoiced separately.

## Google Ads Financial Services Verification UK: Before You Apply

URL: https://ppcconsultancy.uk/guides/google-ads-financial-services-verification-uk/
Description: Google Ads financial services verification for UK firms: FCA authorisation or exemption, the verification deadline, certificates, and why applications fail.

Google will not show financial services ads to people in the UK until the advertiser is verified, and in most cases that means proving FCA authorisation or an exemption, then completing Google's own advertiser verification. The application is a form plus documents, and it fails for mundane reasons: a company name that does not match the register, an account managed by someone outside the firm, or a payments profile in the wrong name. Fix those three before you apply and the process is usually a matter of weeks rather than months.

Messages this guide covers: Advertiser verification, Your account will be paused if you don't complete advertiser verification by the deadline., No, the deadline can't be extended., Is your organisation an agency?, Reset verification, Updating the legal name on a billing profile immediately triggers the need for a new advertiser verification., UK FCA Reference Number (FRN), Eligible (limited).

## Two different checks that owners mix up

When an owner tells me "Google wants us verified", the first job is to find out which verification they mean, because there are two and they are handled in different places.

### Advertiser verification

Google's general programme. It asks who you are and who pays for the ads. Google says all advertisers will eventually be required to complete it, and some accounts are selected sooner, including those running financial services ads, according to the advertiser verification page.

### UK financial services verification

A separate, UK-specific requirement. To show ads for financial services to UK users you must show Google that you are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority or that you qualify for an exemption. Google's August 2021 notice says the requirement covers both FCA-regulated and non-FCA-regulated financial services, and the enforcement dates page gives 6 September 2021 as the UK start date.

You can be fully verified as an advertiser and still be blocked from financial ads, and you can hold an FCA authorisation and still have the account paused because the general verification deadline passed. The two run on separate tracks and both have to be done.

## Who has to pass the UK financial services check

Google's UK financial services policy update of December 2022 is the clearest official statement. Advertisers promoting regulated financial services activities must be authorised by the UK FCA, or be listed on its Financial Services Register as an exempt professional firm or a recognised investment exchange, and must also complete Google's identity verification. The same page brought debt services into scope, with full enforcement from 16 January 2023, and notes that insolvency practitioners can no longer rely on regulation by a Recognised Professional Body to run debt ads in the UK.

The UK Financial Services Verification form on Google's own site lists the three applicant types it accepts. A UK FCA-authorised financial services advertiser. An exempt non-financial services advertiser with a compelling reason to appear for financial searches, such as a search engine or e-commerce platform. An exempt government entity using a .gov.uk domain. The same form has a separate request type for a firm that approves a third party's financial promotions and wants that third party verified, which is how an authorised firm brings an introducer or lead generator into Google Ads.

If you are not sure whether your activity is regulated, the Financial Services Register is the FCA's public record of firms and individuals that are, or have been, authorised. Google reads the same register. If your firm is not on it, or is on it in a different legal name, start there rather than with Google.

### What the FCA side actually requires

The Google form asks you to warrant that any financial services ad placed by an approved advertiser has been approved under section 21(1) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 where required. The FCA's page on approving financial promotions explains the restriction. A person must not communicate an invitation or inducement to engage in investment activity unless they are an authorised person, the promotion has been approved by an authorised person, or an exemption in the Financial Promotion Order 2005 applies. The FCA adds that a firm can only approve a promotion for an unauthorised person if the FCA has granted it permission to do so, or an exemption applies. An ad is a financial promotion, so a mortgage broker's Google ad written by me still has to sit inside that framework, and I would never run one for a firm that cannot show me where its approval comes from.

## The form, the FCA contact and the email domain rule

The UK form is where most first attempts die, so here is what it checks, taken from the form itself.

- Organisation name must exactly match the FCA registration name, including capitalisation and punctuation. The form uses the words "EXACTLY match".

- UK FCA Reference Number (FRN), a 6-digit number, and an organisation address that matches the FCA registration address.

- Google Ads customer ID of the individual account, not a manager account, and a separate form for each customer ID.

- An FCA-registered contact in the Google Ads account. From 26 September 2023 a contact from the FCA-registered entity must be added to the account and must accept the invitation before the form is completed. Google's July 2023 notice says that contact must use the same email domain as the FCA-registered firm.

- Public email domains. If the firm is registered with the FCA under a gmail.com, outlook.com or yahoo.com address, Google's February 2024 update requires a new user added as a Google Ads contact that is an identical match to the FCA registered email address.

- Domains in the format example.com or example.com/subpage. Generic domains such as google.com, youtube.com or facebook.com are not allowed, and apps, videos and social pages need full URLs.

Once notified, the form says you have 30 days to start verification in Google Ads or the account will be paused. That is the line owners tend to miss because the email went to whoever set the account up years ago.

## The general advertiser verification, its deadline and what happens after it

The general programme is simpler but less forgiving. Google's timelines for advertiser verification page splits accounts into two groups. If your notice carries a deadline, the account will be paused if you do not get verified by it, and the page answers the extension question with "No, the deadline can't be extended." If there is no deadline, you can keep running ads while you complete it. Either way Google says review can take up to five working days per task, and in rare cases up to 30 days.

The tasks required for verification page lists what you may be asked for. Questions about your organisation and who pays for the ads. Questions about your business operations, which Google says most advertisers will not see. Documents for the organisation, where the legal name must match the payments profile. A D-U-N-S number, which is optional, with documents required after three unsuccessful attempts. A six-digit code sent by SMS or organisation email to confirm your affiliation. Only a Google Ads account admin can complete these tasks. The same page says certain industries, including financial products, gambling and healthcare, get extra tasks such as questions about the domain's relationship with the industry.

| What you see | What it means for the business | What to do | Official source |

| "Your account will be paused if you don't complete advertiser verification by the deadline." | A hard stop on every campaign in the account on that date. | Have an admin open the Account page under Admin and complete every task before the date. The deadline cannot be extended. | Timelines |

| Verification status not updating after you submit | Review is still running. | Allow up to five working days. Contact support only after that. | Advertiser verification |

| Organisation name "doesn't exactly match the full legal name on the business registration document" | The payments profile name or the form entry differs from Companies House or the FCA register, including suffixes or punctuation. | Correct the payments profile to the registered name, then resubmit. | Business operations issues |

| "Updating the legal name on a billing profile immediately triggers the need for a new advertiser verification." | A rename or restructure sends you back to the start. | Plan the rename, gather the document showing the legal entity is unchanged, verify again. | Advertiser verification |

| "Reset verification" | The wrong organisation was verified or the name shown in ad disclosures must change. | An admin resets under Admin, Policy, Account, and a new deadline is issued. | Change name or ownership |

| "Eligible (limited)" on a healthcare ad | The ad can run only in the locations your certification allows. | Nothing, if the targeting matches the certificate. Otherwise apply for the missing location. | Healthcare and medicines |

## Why UK applications fail, in the order I see them

### The name does not match Companies House or the FCA register

Google's page on issues answering questions about your business operations is explicit. The organisation name must match the registration document, including any suffixes or punctuation, and the payments profile country must match the country on the document. "Smith Financial" on the payments profile and "Smith Financial Planning Ltd" at Companies House is a rejection. You can check what is registered for free on gov.uk, which shows company information such as the registered address and date of incorporation, and the FCA register entry should carry the same legal name. Trading names only count where they appear on the same registration document as the legal name.

### The account is run from outside the firm

When a marketing consultant or a media buyer runs the account, Google wants the relationship explained and documented. The same page lists "Marketing agencies accessing the Google Ads account" among relationships that need supporting documents, such as a contract or a letter on company letterhead. The tasks page adds that someone managing accounts for others must answer Yes to "Is your organisation an agency?" and can either send the client the task link or complete it against the client's own payments profile. For UK financial services the extra rule bites harder. The FCA-registered contact with the firm's own email domain must be in the Google Ads account and must have accepted the invitation. An account with only outside logins cannot pass. This is one reason I insist that the account sits in the client's name with me added as a user, which is also how my Google Ads management engagements are structured anyway.

### The payments profile is in the wrong name or the wrong country

The payments profile is what Google verifies against, so a profile set up by a founder as an individual, or by a parent company abroad, fails even when the trading business is perfectly legitimate. Google's change name or ownership page says the legal name and address in the payments profile must exactly match your government-issued ID or business registration documents, that a VAT number change indicates a new legal entity and cannot be handled as a rename, and that monthly invoicing customers must go through Google Ads support to change the legal name. If the profile is wrong, fix the profile first and only then submit the UK form.

### Proof of address that is too old

Where a proof of address document is requested, Google says it typically needs to have been issued within the last 90 days. A utility bill from the start of the financial year will not do.

## Gambling and healthcare: certification rather than FCA verification

Two other UK sectors need a Google certificate before ads run, and owners often search for "financial services verification" when what they actually need is one of these.

Gambling. Google's gambling and games policy says that in the UK operators of online bingo, sports betting, casino games and lotteries must be registered with the Gambling Commission and hold a valid operating licence number, while raffles and free draws must be registered with the UK Fundraising Regulator or the Scottish Charity Register. Northern Ireland is treated separately, with only state-owned or government-licensed lotteries permitted and offline gambling promotion prohibited. The destination site must show an age warning, addiction resources, terms and conditions and a footer with the licensee name and licence number. Each country requires a separate application, advertisers must recertify after any material change, and the page states that from 19 November 2026 applications move from the Help Centre form into the Google Ads account itself.

Healthcare. The healthcare and medicines policy allows UK online pharmacies with limitations if the pharmacy is registered with the General Pharmaceutical Council, and telemedicine providers if certified under LegitScript's Healthcare Merchant Certification Programme. In both cases ads and landing pages cannot promote prescription drugs, and the page says "Advertisers must also be certified with Google." Addiction services are allowed for government entities only. The prescription drug services page adds the practical rules: apply at the child account level rather than the manager account, submit a separate application per location, and if someone applies on an advertiser's behalf they must send documentation of the relationship with the licence holder. A properly certified ad is then labelled "Eligible (limited)" and runs only where the certificate allows. If you run a clinic or pharmacy, the certification question comes before anything on my healthcare PPC page can be useful to you.

Solicitors are a useful contrast. Legal services do not carry a Google certificate requirement in the UK, so a firm advertising conveyancing or personal injury work faces advertiser verification and ad policy but not a sector gate. Claims management is different because it is FCA-regulated, and a law firm with a claims management arm can find half its account treated as financial services. The PPC for law firms page covers how I separate those campaigns so a verification problem on one side does not pause the other.

## What to do today, and what not to do

- Find the notice. Verification requests arrive as an in-account notification or an email to an admin. Read the deadline before anything else.

- Reconcile three names. Companies House, the FCA register and the Google payments profile must carry the same legal name, suffix and punctuation. Fix the payments profile if it differs.

- Add the FCA-registered contact. Someone with the firm's own email domain, or the identical public address held by the FCA, must be a user in the Google Ads account and must accept the invitation before the UK form goes in.

- Complete the general tasks first. The UK financial services form expects identity verification to be done or under way, and the account pause for a missed general deadline cannot be undone by the FCA form.

- Submit one UK form per customer ID, with the FRN, the registered address and the domains written exactly as the form specifies.

- Do not open a new account. Google treats false information in verification as circumventing systems, which can lead to suspension, and related accounts are suspended together.

Google's general policy page says a non-egregious violation comes with a notification at least seven days before any suspension, and the UK financial services notices repeat that at least seven days' warning is given before suspension for this policy. Use the week. It is enough time to fix a name and add a contact, and it is not enough time to rebuild an account that was closed in a panic.

## Keeping it from happening again

- Keep a note of which email address Google holds for the admin, and make it a shared firm mailbox rather than one person's inbox.

- Treat any change of legal name, VAT number, ownership or payments profile country as a verification event and schedule it, because Google says each of these triggers a new verification or a new profile.

- Keep the FCA-registered contact in the account even if that person leaves the marketing side of the business.

- Store the approval trail for every financial promotion so the section 21 warranty on the form is one you can stand behind.

- Review the FCA register entry when permissions change, since Google reads the register and a lapsed permission can take ads down.

### FAQ

**Do I need FCA authorisation to run Google Ads in the UK?** Only if you advertise financial services. Google's policy requires advertisers promoting regulated financial activities to be FCA-authorised or listed on the Financial Services Register as an exempt firm, and to pass Google's own verification. A plumber or a solicitor advertising conveyancing does not need FCA authorisation, though every advertiser is being brought into the general advertiser verification programme.

**How long does Google Ads financial services verification take in the UK?** Google says each verification task is normally reviewed within five working days and in rare cases up to 30 days. The UK form itself warns that once notified you have 30 days to start verification or the account is paused. Most of the delay I see comes from fixing a name mismatch or waiting for the FCA-registered contact to accept the account invitation.

**Can my marketing consultant complete the verification for me?** Partly. Google lets someone managing the account answer Yes to the agency question and complete tasks against your payments profile, but your organisation's documents must be yours and the UK financial services form requires a contact from your FCA-registered firm, using your firm's email domain, to be a user in the account. The approval of the promotions themselves also has to come from an authorised person under section 21.

**What happens if I miss the advertiser verification deadline?** Google pauses the account, every campaign stops, and the deadline cannot be extended. You can still complete verification afterwards and the account unpauses once it is granted, but the days lost are gone. Opening a fresh account to get round the pause risks suspension of both.

**Why was my verification rejected when my company is genuine?** Nearly always a mismatch. The name on the payments profile differs from Companies House or the FCA register by a suffix or punctuation, the payments profile country differs from the registration document, a proof of address is older than 90 days, or the relationship with the person running the account was not documented. Fix the mismatch and resubmit rather than appealing the decision.

## Google Ads Invoice UK: 2% DST Fee, VAT and 3 Common Mismatches

URL: https://ppcconsultancy.uk/guides/google-ads-invoice-vat-uk/
Description: Google Ads invoices for UK businesses: where to download them, why Google Ireland charges no VAT, the 2% UK DST Fee and what your accountant needs.

Your Google Ads documents live under Billing, then Documents, and are available from the fifth working day of the following month. UK accounts are served by Google Ireland Ltd, which does not add VAT because your billing address is outside the EU, so a VAT registered business accounts for it under the reverse charge. A separate 2% UK DST Fee line appears for ads served in the United Kingdom.

Messages this guide covers: Documents, Download selected, Find in documents, Statements aren't bills, UK DST Fee, Payment threshold, Billing transfers, Payment terms.

## Where the invoice is and how to download it

Google does not email a PDF to most UK advertisers who pay by card or direct debit. The document sits inside the account. Sign in, select the Billing icon, then Documents. Google's Documents page guidance explains that postpay and prepay accounts see statements and local tax documents there, while monthly invoicing accounts see invoices, debit notes and credit notes. Tick the documents you want, choose Download selected, and they arrive as PDFs. There is a Find in documents box at the top right of the table for a specific month.

Timing catches people out at the end of a quarter. The invoice and statement guidance says a statement for a particular month is available from the fifth working day of the following month. If your bookkeeper is chasing the October document on the first of November, it is not late, it does not exist yet. The same page is careful about vocabulary. Statements are not bills. A statement is a summary of billing activity for the period, and whether you receive an invoice or a statement depends on your payment method and billing country.

If the account has changed hands, for instance when billing was moved from a previous supplier to you, the old documents may not show in the main table. Google's Billing transfers page holds the documents from earlier billing setups. This is the single most common reason an accountant tells me a year of invoices is missing. They are not missing, they are under a different setup.

## Who invoices you, and why there is no VAT on it

Google's Taxes in your country page states that your account is served by Google Ireland Ltd and that Google cannot charge VAT if your billing address is in a country that is not part of the European Union. Since the UK left the EU that is the position for a UK billing address. The same page tells you to check with your local tax authority whether you are required to self-assess VAT in your country. In the UK that self-assessment is the reverse charge.

HMRC's VAT Notice 741A, section 5, sets out how it works. When a UK VAT registered business buys a service from a supplier that belongs outside the UK, the customer must act as if they are both the supplier and the recipient. You add output tax on the full value of the supply to Box 1 of your return and claim the same amount as input tax in Box 4, with the value of the supply in Boxes 6 and 7. If your business can recover all its input tax, the net cost is nil. The standard rate used for that calculation is 20%.

Two practical consequences follow. First, the invoice total is the net figure, so do not multiply it by anything before entering it in the purchase ledger. Second, the reverse charge counts towards your turnover for registration. Paragraph 5.7 of Notice 741A says the value of general rule services received from overseas suppliers must be added to the value of your own taxable supplies when determining whether you should be registered, even if you make no taxable supplies yourself. A business that is near the £90,000 registration threshold should ask its accountant how the Google spend affects that calculation before it grows the budget. I raise this on the first call with any non registered client, because an unexpected registration is a worse surprise than any auction.

Google asks for a VAT number in the payments profile when the account is created. Entering it correctly is what tells Google you are a business customer. The billing options page says that if your account is served by Google Ireland and you pay by credit card, Google will charge 20% VAT to customers with a personal tax status or an individual entrepreneur status that is not VAT registered, which is why a sole trader who signed up with a personal profile sometimes sees tax on a document while a limited company does not.

## The 2% UK DST Fee line

Since 1 November 2020 Google has added a line to UK documents that confuses almost every new client. The Jurisdiction specific surcharges page says a 2% UK DST Fee will be added to your next invoice or statement for ads served in the United Kingdom, driven by the Digital Services Tax in that jurisdiction. It appears as a separate line item per jurisdiction, is calculated on the cost of ads served in the UK, is added on top of any account budget you have set, and applicable taxes are charged in addition to it. For postpay accounts it is added once at the end of every month.

The tax itself is not on you. The government's Digital Services Tax policy paper describes a 2% tax on the revenues of search engines, social media services and online marketplaces that derive value from UK users, applying to revenue earned from 1 April 2020, and only for groups with worldwide digital revenues above £500 million and UK user revenues above £25 million. Google pays that. The fee on your invoice is Google passing its cost on to advertisers, which it is free to do, and which you cannot opt out of.

What you can do is budget for it. If a campaign is set to spend a fixed amount a month on UK traffic, the document will be that amount plus 2%, and your accountant will apply the reverse charge to the invoiced total. Ads served to users outside the UK do not carry the UK fee, though other jurisdictions have their own surcharges listed on the same Google page.

## Monthly invoicing or automatic payments

Most UK small and medium businesses are on what Google now calls postpay, formerly automatic payments. The payment settings page describes it as accruing advertising costs, then having them charged automatically on the first day of each month or whenever the account reaches a predetermined amount known as the payment threshold. That threshold rises as the account proves itself, which is why the card is charged several times in a busy month and the amounts do not line up with calendar months.

Monthly invoicing is a credit line rather than a card. Google's monthly invoicing page lists the requirements, which include being registered as a business for at least one year, having an active Google Ads account in good standing for a minimum of six months, and spending at least $5,000 USD a month, or the local equivalent, in any three of the last twelve months. Payment terms are typically 30 days from the invoice, invoices are emailed by the fifth working day of each month, and if you exceed your terms or credit line your ads may be slowed or stopped. The bill to details on the account must match the company that applied for the credit line, which is the step that trips up groups with several trading names.

| What the document or screen says | What it means | What to do | Official reference |

| Documents | The page under Billing where statements and invoices live | Tick the months you need and choose Download selected | About the Documents page |

| Statements aren't bills | A statement is a summary of activity, not a request for payment | Use it for the ledger. Payment already happened by card or direct debit | Get an invoice, statement or payment receipt |

| UK DST Fee | A 2% surcharge on ads served in the UK | Budget 2% above the campaign spend. It cannot be removed | Jurisdiction specific surcharges |

| Payment threshold | The accrued amount that triggers a card charge before month end | Expect several charges a month. Reconcile to the statement, not the card | About payment settings |

| Billing transfers | Documents from an earlier billing setup, for instance a previous supplier | Look here when a year of invoices seems to be missing | About the Billing transfers page |

| Payment terms | Days allowed to pay a monthly invoice, typically 30 | Only applies to monthly invoicing accounts | About monthly invoicing |

| Unpaid balance or concerns about future payments | A billing suspension reason, usually a declined card | An admin must confirm the payment method or pay. Verification may be requested within 30 days | Billing and payment suspensions |

## What your accountant needs from you

Accountants do not need access to Google Ads, and I would not give it to them, because a billing login is also a campaign login. What they need is a predictable monthly pack.

- The monthly statement or invoice PDF from Documents, downloaded after the fifth working day.

- Confirmation that the supplier is Google Ireland Ltd and that the supply is a reverse charge service, so it is coded to the right VAT treatment rather than to zero rated or exempt. HMRC's notice gives the box numbers above.

- The card or bank statement lines for the same month, because on postpay several charges add up to one statement.

- A note of any UK DST Fee line, so the 2% is treated as part of the cost of the advertising and not as a tax paid to HMRC.

- If you use a manager or consultant, a clear statement that ad spend is paid by you directly to Google and the management fee is a separate UK invoice. That separation is how I work, and the pricing page explains why the two should never be mixed in one bill.

Once that pack is agreed, the only recurring question is why the campaign screen and the invoice disagree, which is the subject of the next section.

## Three reasons the invoice does not match the campaign spend

Owners compare the Cost column in Google Ads with the document and assume something is wrong. Usually three things are happening at once.

- The DST Fee and taxes sit outside the campaign figures. The campaign screen shows media cost only. Google's surcharge page says the fee is added on top of your budget and that taxes are charged in addition, so the document will always be at least 2% higher than the campaign total for UK traffic.

- Charge dates do not follow calendar months. On postpay the card is charged at each payment threshold and on the first of the month, so a month with three charges on the bank statement may correspond to one Google statement. Reconcile the statement to the sum of the charges, not to any single one.

- Adjustments arrive later. Invalid click credits, promotional credits and overdelivery adjustments are posted as separate lines, sometimes in the following month's document. If the document is lower than the campaign spend, look for a credit line before assuming an error.

None of this is a sign the account is being overcharged, but a persistent gap that the three explanations do not cover is worth a look, and it is one of the first things I reconcile in ongoing PPC management. Google's billing suspensions page also makes an important point for anyone tempted to dispute a card charge with the bank. Requesting a chargeback against a legitimate balance can lead to the account being suspended, so query it with Google first.

## Keeping the billing side quiet

- Use a company card or a direct debit, in the company name, with an expiry date in a diary. In the accounts I have inherited, a declined card is the usual cause of a billing suspension.

- Have at least two admins on the account, so the person who can confirm a payment method is not on holiday when Google asks.

- Download the statements quarterly rather than at year end. Documents older than the current setup move to Billing transfers.

- Check the VAT number in the payments profile once a year, and after any change of legal entity.

- Ask about monthly invoicing only when you meet all the published requirements. A refused application is not harmful, but it is a month of paperwork for nothing.

If a question here is specific to your books, the FAQ page covers how fees, spend and VAT are handled when I manage an account, and your accountant should have the final word on the VAT treatment.

### FAQ

**Does Google charge VAT on Google Ads in the UK?** No. Google's own tax page says UK accounts are served by Google Ireland Ltd and that Google cannot charge VAT where the billing address is outside the EU. A UK VAT registered business accounts for the VAT itself under the reverse charge described in HMRC Notice 741A, with no net cost if it recovers all its input tax.

**What is the UK DST Fee on my Google Ads invoice?** A 2% surcharge Google adds to ads served in the United Kingdom, in place since 1 November 2020, to recover its Digital Services Tax cost. It appears as a separate line, is added on top of your campaign budget, and cannot be switched off.

**Where do I download my Google Ads invoice?** Sign in, select the Billing icon, then Documents. Tick the months you want and choose Download selected to get PDFs. A statement for a month is available from the fifth working day of the following month, and older documents from a previous billing setup are under Billing transfers.

**Can my business get monthly invoicing from Google Ads?** Only if it meets Google's published requirements, which include at least one year as a registered business, six months with an account in good standing, and spending at least $5,000 USD a month in any three of the last twelve months. Terms are typically 30 days, and Google reviews your credit history before approving.

**Why is my Google Ads invoice higher than the spend in the account?** The campaign screen shows media cost only. The document adds the 2% UK DST Fee on UK traffic, and on card accounts several threshold charges in a month add up to one statement. Credits for invalid clicks or promotions can also post in a later month, which makes a document lower than expected.

## Google Ads Not Showing? What Each Status Really Means

URL: https://ppcconsultancy.uk/guides/google-ads-not-showing-uk/
Description: Google ads not showing: what Limited by budget, Eligible (limited), Learning and Under review mean for a UK business, and when more budget is the wrong fix.

In most accounts I open, the ad is showing and the owner simply cannot see it, because searching for your own ad is not a reliable test. When ads genuinely are not running, the status column in Google Ads already names the reason: Limited by budget, Eligible (limited), Not eligible, Pending or Under review. Each of those has a different fix, and only one of them is more money.

Messages this guide covers: Eligible, Eligible (limited), Limited by budget, Not eligible, Pending, Ended, Paused, Under review.

## First, prove the ad is actually not showing

An owner types their own service into Google on a Tuesday evening, sees a competitor and not themselves, and concludes the campaign is broken. It usually is not. Your ad may be outside its schedule, the daily budget may have been spent by lunchtime, Google may be rotating ads, or your own repeated searches without clicks may have taught the system that you are not a buyer. Google's Ad Preview and Diagnosis tool exists for exactly this. It shows a preview of the results page for a search term, location and device, and Google says it "avoids accumulating ad impressions and impacting your performance statistics", which a manual search does not. It also warns that your ad may stop appearing in the preview once the campaign has reached its average daily budget, which is the most common honest answer to "why can't I see my ad at 6pm".

The tool sits under Tools and then Troubleshooting. If it says the ad is not showing and gives "Reason unknown", Google lists two common causes: the campaign is in a learning period after a bidding change, or the keyword has low search volume and will not trigger a preview. Before diagnosing anything else, the same page says to check the account itself, because ads do not serve while an account is in billing verification or temporarily suspended for security reasons.

So the order is: run the preview tool for your real location, read the status column, then decide. The rest of this guide is the status column.

## The campaign statuses, in Google's words

Google defines campaign statuses on its campaign status page and its about campaign statuses page. The ones that matter when nothing seems to be running are below, with what each means for the business rather than for the person operating the account.

| Status shown | Google's definition | What it means for you | Right fix |

| Eligible | "Your campaign is active and can show ads." | Nothing is wrong at campaign level. If you cannot see the ad, the problem is schedule, location, budget pacing or your test method. | Use Ad Preview and Diagnosis, not a Google search. |

| Eligible (limited) | "only showing ads occasionally due to budget constraints or a limited bid strategy." | Ads run, but Google is rationing them. Impressions arrive in bursts and then stop. | Read the bid strategy status before adding budget. Often the target is too tight, not the budget too small. |

| Limited by budget | "The campaign is active and can show ads, but not as often as it could due to budget constraints." | There is more demand than money. You are missing searches you could have won. | Decide whether those extra searches are worth having. More budget is only right if the existing clicks convert. |

| Not eligible | "there are no ad groups, all ad groups are paused or deleted" (or all ads or keywords are paused or deleted). | The campaign is a shell. Something inside it was paused or removed, often during a clean-up. | Open the campaign and look at ad groups, ads and keywords for the paused or removed items. |

| Pending | "scheduled to begin at a future date." | Someone set a start date. Nothing will run until it arrives. | Change the start date if that was a mistake. |

| Ended | "it's past its scheduled end date." | An end date from a previous promotion or a test is still on the campaign. | Remove or move the end date. |

| Paused | "Your campaign is inactive because you paused it." | Someone with access paused it. Check the change history to see who. | Resume it, and find out why it was paused first. |

Two more strings appear at ad level rather than campaign level and are covered by Google's ad status page. "Under review" means the ad is being checked against policy, and Google says most ads are reviewed within one working day, to check the status if it takes more than two full working days, and to contact support if it takes more than a week. "Disapproved" means the review found a policy violation and the ad cannot show anywhere. A disapproved ad will not run until it is fixed and reviewed again, and Google's disapproved ad page limits each ad to three appeals with at least 24 hours between appeals on the same ads.

## Learning, Limited and Misconfigured: the bid strategy column

People search for "learning limited" because they see two words in two columns at once: a campaign status of "Eligible (limited)" and a bid strategy status of "Learning". Google documents the bid strategy statuses on its bid strategy statuses page.

### Learning

Google says there may be minor performance fluctuations as it optimises bids after a new strategy or after campaigns and keywords are added or removed. Its dedicated Smart Bidding learning page says the status "never lasts more than seven days", is triggered only by a new strategy, a composition change or a significant goal change, and is never triggered by budget, target, creative or targeting changes. Judge results over two conversion cycles or two weeks, whichever is longer.

### Limited

Google lists four causes. Inventory, meaning available search volume. Bid limits that stop bids being fully optimised. Budget constrained, where many of the keywords are Limited by budget. And the bidding strategy itself, where a target CPA is too low or a target ROAS is too high for what the market will give.

### Misconfigured

Conversion-based strategies do not have the right conversion actions set up, or a Maximise strategy is sharing a budget with a different strategy. Google's campaign statuses page adds a note that "Eligible (misconfigured)" usually means no biddable conversions were recorded in the last 28 days.

This matters for the owner because the fix for each is different and none of them is "spend more". A Learning status means wait and stop changing things. A Limited status caused by a bid limit or a tight target means loosen the target, not the wallet. A Misconfigured status means the tracking is broken, which is a PPC audit finding rather than a bidding problem, and raising budget on a campaign that cannot see its own conversions only buys more untracked clicks.

## Why "Limited by budget" is a decision, not an error

Google's page on fixing Limited by budget says the status appears when your average daily budget is lower than the recommended amount, and offers a budget simulator to show how much exposure a different budget might buy. It lists two responses: a higher budget to increase clicks, or lower bid adjustments to get more clicks within the same budget. Notice what it does not say. It does not say the campaign is broken. The campaign is working and the market has more searches than you chose to pay for.

Whether to buy them depends on one question: are the clicks you already buy turning into enquiries at a cost you would pay again? If the answer is yes, Limited by budget is the best status in the account because it tells you growth is available. If the answer is no, or you do not know because tracking is unreliable, more budget scales the waste. In audits for UK small businesses this is the single most common place money is lost. The campaign shows the red "Limited by budget" bubble, someone raises the budget, and the extra spend goes to the same broad match terms that were not converting at the lower budget either. The Google Ads for small business page explains how I size a budget from conversion data rather than from Google's recommendation.

There is a second reason to pause before paying. The same Google page says that from 17 August 2026 Google is updating how its bidding systems optimise budget-limited campaigns running Target CPA, Target ROAS, and Target CPC for Demand Gen, and that this may cause temporary performance and traffic fluctuations. A bid target adjustment tool became available on 6 July 2026, and Google says it will not change your budgets or targets for you. If a campaign that was fine in spring started behaving oddly in late summer, that change is a more likely cause than anything you did.

### How the daily budget really spends

Owners also misread normal pacing as "not spending" or "overspending". Google's overdelivery page says that on a given day a campaign might spend up to twice your average daily budget, and that at the end of the month you will have spent no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget. A £50 daily budget can take £100 on a busy Monday and £15 on a quiet Sunday. If you check only on the quiet day, the ad looks absent. If you check only the busy day, you think you are being overcharged. Neither is true.

## Location and schedule mistakes common in UK accounts

When the status column says Eligible and the preview tool still shows nothing for you, the campaign settings are usually to blame. Three patterns repeat in UK accounts.

### The location setting reaches the wrong people, or excludes you

Google's location targeting page describes two target options. "Presence or Interest" reaches people in your targeted locations and people who have shown interest in them, and Google recommends it as a best practice on Search. "Presence" reaches only people physically in the location. For a Manchester accountant, Presence or Interest means a person in Lisbon researching UK accountants can see and click the ad, while Presence means a Mancunian searching from a hotel in Lisbon cannot. Neither is wrong, but owners rarely know which one is set, and a sudden fall in impressions after an "optimisation" is often someone switching the setting. Radius targeting has a minimum of 1 km, so a tight radius around a shop in a dense town can be far smaller than the trade area it serves.

### The ad schedule runs on the account time zone, which may not be London

Google's ad schedule setup page states that "Ad schedules are set based on your account's time zone", with a maximum of six ad schedules per day for each campaign, and a schedule that runs past midnight has to be split across two days. The account time zone is the trap. Google's time zone setting page says it is set when the account is created and that time zone changes are no longer supported in standard serving accounts. Accounts opened by a founder while living abroad, or set up by a supplier overseas, keep that time zone forever. A 9 to 5 schedule on an account that thinks it is in New York runs from 2pm to 10pm in the UK, and the owner who searches at 10am sees nothing.

### Spending limits that used to be campaign budgets

Monthly spending limits set at account level, campaign end dates left over from a Christmas push, and ad groups paused during a seasonal clean-up all produce a campaign that looks live and serves nothing. The change history in Google Ads shows who did what and when, and I read it before I change anything.

## What to do today, in order

- Check the account before the campaign. Billing verification, a payment that failed, or a security hold stops every ad. The Ad Preview page itself says to check account status first.

- Run Ad Preview and Diagnosis for your real keyword, your real town and mobile. Stop searching for yourself on Google.

- Read the campaign status and the bid strategy status together. Eligible plus Learning means wait. Eligible (limited) plus Limited means loosen targets or accept the limit. Not eligible means something inside was paused or removed.

- Open the ad statuses. Under review older than two working days gets a status check. Disapproved gets fixed and resubmitted, with at most three appeals per ad.

- Check location option, schedule and the account time zone before concluding that demand is missing.

- Only then look at budget, and only if the clicks you already buy are converting.

What not to do: do not create a duplicate campaign to "restart" it, which resets learning and splits your data, and do not change the budget, the target and the keywords in the same afternoon, because you will never know which change worked. If several of these are true at once, the account has drifted and a structured review is cheaper than another month of guessing. That is what the audit is for, and the Google Ads management page describes how the weekly checks stop the drift coming back.

## Keeping ads visible without babysitting them

- Check the status column once a week, not the search results page. The preview tool is for spot checks.

- Leave Smart Bidding alone while it shows Learning, which Google says never lasts more than seven days, and make one change at a time.

- Write down the account time zone and the location option on the first page of your campaign notes so the next person does not guess.

- Remove end dates and seasonal schedules when the season ends, not when you notice the silence.

- Treat "Limited by budget" as a quarterly decision backed by cost per enquiry, not as an alert to act on the same day.

- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1722120?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1704381?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6263057?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/2616012?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1704443?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1722043?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6372656?hl=en-GB

### FAQ

**Why is my Google ad not showing when I search for it?** Because a Google search is not a test. Your budget may have been spent for the day, the campaign may be outside its schedule, your location setting may not include where you are standing, or Google may simply not have entered that auction for you. Use the Ad Preview and Diagnosis tool inside Google Ads, which Google says avoids adding impressions and skewing your statistics.

**What does Limited by budget mean in Google Ads?** Google's definition is that the campaign is active and can show ads but not as often as it could because of budget constraints. There is more demand than you have chosen to pay for. It is a signal of available growth, not a fault, and whether to act on it depends on whether the clicks you already buy are converting at a price you would pay again.

**How long does Learning last in Google Ads?** Google's Smart Bidding learning page says the Learning status never lasts more than seven days and is triggered by a new strategy, a change to what is inside the strategy or a significant change to the conversion goals. Budget and target changes do not trigger it. Google then advises judging results over two conversion cycles or a two-week window, whichever is longer.

**Why does my campaign say Eligible but get no impressions?** Eligible only means nothing is blocking the campaign itself. Look at the ad statuses for Under review or Disapproved, the bid strategy status for Limited or Misconfigured, the location option, the ad schedule and the account time zone. In UK accounts the time zone and the location option explain most of these cases.

**Should I raise my budget to get my ads showing?** Only if the status is Limited by budget and the existing clicks convert at an acceptable cost. If the status is Learning, Not eligible, Pending, Under review or Disapproved, more money changes nothing. If the bid strategy is Limited by its targets, loosening the target is the fix, and if it is Misconfigured the problem is tracking rather than spend.

## Google Ads Not Working: Account, Website or Market, Not Luck

URL: https://ppcconsultancy.uk/guides/google-ads-not-working-uk/
Description: Google Ads not working for your UK business? Clicks and spend but no enquiries. Three numbers to request, the four usual causes and when to pause.

When Google Ads shows clicks and spend but the phone does not ring, the cause is almost always one of four things: the searches the ads are matching, where and when they run, the page people land on, or the way results are measured. You do not need to log in to find out which. Three numbers and one report, requested from whoever runs the account, will tell you in half an hour, and Google's own pages set how long "still learning" is allowed to last.

Messages this guide covers: Learning, Conversions, Invalid clicks, Invalid activity, Limited by budget, Eligible (limited).

## What to ask for, without logging in

Owners often feel they cannot judge a Google Ads account because they do not understand the interface. You do not need to. Ask the person running it for three numbers for the last 30 days and one export, and read them the way you read a bank statement.

### 1. Spend and clicks

Total cost and total clicks for the period, by campaign. This tells you what you bought. Google's budget page says a campaign may spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day and no more than 30.4 times that budget in a month, so compare the month, not a single day.

### 2. Conversions, and what they are

The number of conversions and, more importantly, the list of conversion actions being counted. If "page view" or "button click" is on that list, the conversion number is not enquiries. Google's conversion data page explains that the "Conversions" column counts whatever actions are set as primary, and that this is the column Google bids on.

### 3. Enquiries you actually received

Your own count of calls, forms and emails that came from the ads, from your inbox, phone log or CRM. The gap between this number and number 2 is the measurement problem, and it is usually the first thing I fix.

The one export is the search terms report. Google's search terms report page describes it as the list of actual searches that triggered your ads, as opposed to the keywords someone typed into the account, and notes that terms without enough query activity are omitted for privacy. Ask for it as a spreadsheet sorted by cost. If whoever runs the account hesitates to send it, that is itself an answer.

### What a healthy search terms report looks like

Read the top 20 rows by cost. In a healthy account for a UK service business, nearly every row is something a paying customer would type: the service, the town, a problem the service solves, a "near me", a competitor you would be happy to be compared with. In a sick account the expensive rows are jobs ("plumber vacancies"), training ("how to become"), DIY ("fix boiler myself"), the wrong country, or famous brands you do not sell. Google's keyword matching page says broad match is the default match type for every keyword and that it may show ads on searches "that don't contain the direct meaning of your keywords". That one default explains most sick reports.

## Account, website or market: the half-hour verdict

With the three numbers and the report in front of you, the diagnosis falls out.

- It is the account if the expensive search terms are wrong, if the campaign runs outside your area or your hours, or if conversions are counting things that are not enquiries. Clicks are being bought from the wrong people. Nothing on your website will fix this.

- It is the website if the search terms look right, the clicks land on your site, and you still receive nothing. People wanted what you sell, arrived, and left. The page is the problem: slow, no phone number above the fold, a form that fails on mobile, a price that frightens, or a homepage where a service page should be.

- It is the market only if the search terms are right, the page is sound, the measurement reconciles with your inbox, and the cost of each enquiry is still more than an enquiry is worth to you. This is the rarest of the three in UK small-business accounts, and it is the only one where stopping is the correct answer.

"It is still learning" belongs to none of these categories. It is a status, not a diagnosis, and the next section shows how long Google itself allows it to last.

## The four usual causes in UK small-business accounts

In the accounts I audit for UK businesses, the same four causes account for nearly every "Google Ads is not working" conversation. Each has a sign the owner can see without logging in, a question to ask, and a Google page that settles the argument.

| Cause | Sign you can see | Question to ask | Official reference |

| Search terms | Expensive rows in the search terms report that no customer would type. | "Which match type are the keywords on, and when were negatives last added?" | Broad match is the default and can match searches without the keyword's meaning: keyword matching. Negatives exclude searches but do not block close variants: negative keywords. |

| Location and schedule | Enquiries from the wrong part of the country, or calls arriving when nobody answers. | "Is the location option Presence or Presence or Interest, and what time zone is the account set to?" | Two location options exist, and Google recommends Presence or Interest on Search: location targeting. Ad schedules follow the account time zone: ad schedules. |

| Landing page | Right searches, clicks arriving, nothing in the inbox. | "Which page does each ad land on, and have you tested the form on a phone this month?" | Google's destination requirements policy also disapproves ads whose page does not work or whose phone number is unverified. |

| Measurement | The conversion number and your inbox do not agree in either direction. | "Which conversion actions are primary, and when did the tag last record a real enquiry?" | Reporting lags run 24 to 48 hours and the Conversions column is what bidding optimises towards: conversion data. |

The measurement row deserves a word. When the tag counts page views as conversions, Google's bidding chases page views and reports success while the business gets nothing. When the tag is broken and counts nothing, the bidding has no target and spends blindly. Either way the account looks like it is "not converting" when the truth is that it is not measuring. The conversion tracking page describes how I rebuild that layer so the number in Google Ads is the number in your inbox.

## What "still learning" really means, in Google's words

"Learning" is a real status. It is also the most overused excuse in paid search. Google's About Smart Bidding learning page says the Learning status "never lasts more than seven days" and that ads keep running normally during it. The same page lists only three triggers: a new or reactivated bid strategy, a composition change where campaigns, ad groups or keywords are added or removed, and a significant change to the conversion goals being optimised. It then states that changes to budgets, targets, creative or targeting settings never trigger a Learning status.

So when you are told that a budget change or a new ad "put the campaign back into learning", that is not what Google says happens. Google's guidance on judging results is also specific: allow one to two conversion cycles for the system to converge on a new goal, then evaluate over two conversion cycles or a two-week window, whichever is longer. Its Smart Bidding page adds that performance should be judged over periods with at least 30 conversions, and that Target ROAS wants around 50. A campaign producing three enquiries a month is not "learning", it is starved, and Google's own learning page notes that very restrictive settings such as low daily budgets slow the ramp-up.

The practical rule I give owners: a Learning status older than a week, or a learning excuse offered for the third month running, is a sign that nobody has looked at the search terms.

## Spam and fake leads: what Google publishes about invalid traffic

A different complaint is clicks that convert into junk: forms filled by bots, calls from overseas call centres offering "SEO services", enquiries from people who clearly never searched for you. Two separate things are going on, and Google only takes responsibility for one of them.

The first is invalid clicks. Google's invalid traffic page defines them as clicks and impressions that do not reflect genuine user interest, including intentionally fraudulent traffic and accidental or duplicate clicks, and says "You won't be charged for invalid clicks or impressions". Detected clicks are filtered before billing and credits appear as "Invalid activity" under Adjustments in the Billing summary. You can add the "Invalid clicks" column to campaign reports to see how many were filtered, according to Google's invalid clicks definition. If you suspect clicks Google missed, the same page says the click quality form accepts investigation requests about "invalid clicks, poor quality form submissions, clicks outside location targeting or sudden short-term cost increases", and the invalid traffic page says investigations cover the past 60 days and take several working days.

The second is spam that arrives after a real click, or through your website without any click at all. A bot that fills your contact form found the form, not the ad, and Google will not credit you for it. The fixes are on your side: a form that validates, a spam filter on the form, a phone number that is not scraped, and a conversion set-up that only counts an enquiry when a human has submitted something sensible. The click quality form explicitly includes poor quality form submissions, so when junk clearly follows ad clicks it is worth filing, but the lasting fix is to stop counting junk as a conversion so Google stops optimising towards it.

Two owner-level checks catch most fake lead problems. Ask where the enquiries say they are, and compare that with the location setting. Ask what time they arrive, and compare that with the schedule and the account time zone, which Google's time zone page says cannot be changed on a standard account once set.

## Pause, change who runs it, or stop

Once you know which of the three it is, the decision is simpler than it feels.

- Pause when the measurement does not reconcile with your inbox. Spending while blind is the one case where a pause costs nothing, because you were not learning anything from the spend anyway. Fix the tracking, then restart. Pausing to "save money" when the search terms are the problem only delays the same fix.

- Change who runs it when the search terms report is bad and the person responsible either did not send it or defended it. A report full of job seekers and DIY queries after three months is not a learning problem. Ask for a written plan with dates before you move, so the handover is judged against something.

- Stop only when the account, the page and the measurement are all sound and the cost per real enquiry is still above what an enquiry is worth. That verdict needs clean data for at least the window Google itself uses to judge bidding, two conversion cycles or two weeks, and in my experience most owners who reach it discover they never had clean data to begin with.

If you cannot tell which of the three applies, a short independent review of the account is cheaper than another month of spend. That is exactly what a PPC audit is for, and it is written for the owner rather than for the person who built the campaigns.

## Questions to put to whoever runs it before paying another month

These are the questions I would want to be asked if I were running your account. The answers should be specific, written and quick.

- Send me the search terms report for the last 30 days sorted by cost. Which of the top 20 rows would you remove today, and why have they not been removed?

- Which conversion actions are set as primary, and what did each of them count last month? How does that reconcile with the enquiries in my inbox?

- What location option is the campaign on, what time zone is the account set to, and what is the schedule?

- Which page does each ad land on? When did you last submit the form from a phone?

- Which bid strategy is in use, when did it last show Learning, and what triggered it? Google says the status never lasts more than seven days and is not triggered by budget or target changes.

- How many invalid clicks were filtered last month, and have you filed a click quality request for the junk enquiries I forwarded?

- What will be different in the account thirty days from now, and how will we both know?

Anyone competent can answer these in an afternoon. Anyone who cannot is telling you where the problem is. The Google Ads management page sets out how I report these same points every month, in writing, so that the question never has to be asked.

## Keeping it working once it works

- Read the search terms report monthly, even if someone else runs the account. It is the one document that cannot be dressed up.

- Reconcile conversions against your inbox or CRM every month. The two numbers should move together.

- Treat any change in your trading area, opening hours or phone handling as a campaign change and tell whoever runs the account the same day.

- Keep one landing page per service, and submit its form yourself after any website update.

- Judge results over the window Google uses, two conversion cycles or two weeks at minimum, and never on a single day's spend.

### FAQ

**Why is Google Ads not converting for my business?** In UK small-business accounts the cause is usually one of four: the ads are matching searches no customer would type, the campaign runs in the wrong place or at the wrong hours, the landing page loses people who did want the service, or the conversion tracking counts the wrong things. Ask for the search terms report and the list of conversion actions and you will usually see which one it is.

**How long does Google Ads take to work?** Google's own page on Smart Bidding learning says the Learning status never lasts more than seven days, and that results should be judged over two conversion cycles or a two-week window, whichever is longer. If you are told an account is still learning after several months, the explanation is not learning.

**Does Google charge for spam clicks and fake leads?** Google says you are not charged for clicks it detects as invalid, and credits appear as Invalid activity in the Billing summary. Spam that arrives through your website form after a genuine click, or with no click at all, is not covered, so the fix is on your side: form validation, spam filtering and not counting junk submissions as conversions. You can also file a click quality request, which covers poor quality form submissions and clicks outside your location targeting.

**Is Google Ads worth it for a small UK business?** It is worth it when the cost of a real enquiry is below what an enquiry is worth to you, measured with tracking that reconciles with your inbox. Most accounts that look unprofitable have never been measured properly, so the honest answer requires fixing measurement first and then judging over at least two weeks of clean data.

**Should I pause Google Ads if it is not working?** Pause when the conversion data does not match the enquiries you actually receive, because spending blind teaches you nothing. Change who runs it when the search terms report is poor and nobody is acting on it. Stop only when the account, the page and the measurement are sound and the cost per enquiry is still too high.

## How to Advertise Your Business in the UK: Free, Paid and the Rules

URL: https://ppcconsultancy.uk/guides/how-to-advertise-your-business-uk/
Description: How to advertise your business in the UK: the free Google listing, which paid adverts suit which business, and the advertising, email and cookie rules to follow.

Most advice on advertising a business is a list of twenty channels. An owner needs something shorter: what to do first, what costs nothing, when paying for adverts makes sense, and which UK rules apply from the first day. This guide follows that order and quotes the official pages, from Google, GOV.UK, the Advertising Standards Authority and the Information Commissioner's Office.

Messages this guide covers: Business Profile, Search campaigns, Performance Max, Local Services Ads, Advertiser verification.

## Start with what is free: the Business Profile

Before any paid advert, claim the listing Google already shows for your business. Google's Business Profile page says "you can manage how your business shows up on Maps and Search at no charge", whether "you own a shop front business or provide services where your customers are". The page for adding or claiming a profile repeats it: "You can add or claim your business at no charge."

You then have to verify it. Google's verification page says "Verification methods are automatically determined by Google and can't be changed", and that you may need more than one method. Do this first, because several paid options depend on a verified profile, and because for a local business the profile is often what a customer sees before the website.

## Which paid adverts fit which business

Google's campaign type page says you choose "based on your marketing goals, brand strategy and how much time you can invest". In plain terms:

| Your situation | Where to start | Why |

| People search for what you do when they need it: a solicitor, a plumber, an accountant, a clinic | A Search campaign in Google Ads | Google describes these as "Text ads on search results". You appear when someone types the need, and pay when they click. |

| You sell products online | Shopping, or Performance Max with a product feed | Google lists these as "Product listings on Google". The advert is the product, its photo and its price. |

| You are a trade or home service | Local Services Ads, alongside Search | You pay per lead and Google verifies the business first. See the guide to Local Services Ads verification in the UK. |

| Nobody searches for your product yet | Paid social, such as Meta Ads on Facebook and Instagram | Search can only reach demand that exists. A new kind of product has to be shown to people before they look for it. |

| You have very little time and a small budget | The Business Profile first, then one tightly targeted Search campaign | One campaign you understand is worth more than five you do not. |

Two cautions. Performance Max is described by Google as "a goal-based campaign type that allows performance advertisers to access all Google Ads inventory from a single campaign". That reach is useful once conversion tracking works. Without it, the campaign has nothing reliable to aim at. And for professional services, Google's UK requirements page says professional services in Local Services Ads "are currently being piloted and are only available in Greater London".

What a click is likely to cost in your trade is covered in the guide to what Google Ads costs in the UK.

## The rules every UK advert has to follow

GOV.UK's guide to marketing and advertising law starts with a short list. All marketing and advertising must be "an accurate description of the product or service", "legal", "decent", "truthful", "honest" and "socially responsible".

Behind that list are two layers. The first is the law. The same guide's page on regulations that affect advertising says you cannot mislead or harass consumers by "including false or deceptive messages", "leaving out important information" or "using aggressive sales techniques". It also states the penalty for enforcement action: "up to £300,000 or 10% of your global turnover, whichever is higher". When you advertise to other businesses, you must not make misleading comparisons with competitors, which includes "using a competitor's logo or trademark, or something very similar".

The second layer is the advertising code. GOV.UK's page on advertising codes of practice says the CAP non-broadcast code covers "non-broadcast advertising (for example print, online), sales promotion and direct marketing", and that "The rules are enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority". The first rule on misleading advertising in the CAP Code reads: "Marketing communications must not materially mislead or be likely to do so."

Owners are often surprised by how far this reaches. The ASA's complaints page lists what it covers online, including "Claims made on a company's website or app" and "Paid-for search listings". So the wording of a Google advert and the claims on the page it leads to are both in scope. In practice: do not write "best", "cheapest" or "number one" unless you hold the evidence, and make sure the price or offer in the advert is the one the visitor finds on the page.

Some sectors carry extra rules. GOV.UK names food, alcohol, beauty products, environmentally friendly products, medicines and tobacco. Google adds its own checks for some advertisers, covered in the guide to financial services verification.

## Email, text, phone and cookies

Advertising usually leads to a list of contacts, and the rules change when you contact people directly.

- Email and text to individuals need consent. The ICO's guidance on electronic mail marketing says "You must not send marketing emails or texts to individuals without specific consent. There is a limited exception for your own previous customers, often called the 'soft opt-in'."

- Sole traders count as individuals. The same page says "Sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals". It also says "You can email or text any corporate body", and recommends keeping a list of businesses that object.

- Bought lists do not get the exception. The ICO says the soft opt-in "does not apply to prospective customers or new contacts (eg from bought-in lists)".

- Phone calls have a register. GOV.UK's page on direct marketing says it is illegal to phone someone registered with the Telephone Preference Service without their permission, and that "You can be fined up to £500,000 for each unsolicited phonecall."

- Every marketing email needs a way out. GOV.UK: "Every marketing email you send must give the person the ability to opt out of (or 'unsubscribe from') further emails."

- Cookies need a clear notice and a choice. GOV.UK: "You must tell visitors to your website how your site uses cookies, and ask if they want to accept them." This is the consent banner, and it affects what your adverts can measure. See the guide to conversions not tracking.

## Before the first paid click

- Expect to be verified. Google's advertiser verification page says it "will notify you via an in-account notification or an email when you need to complete advertiser verification and what your deadline will be", and that "some of your ads may be restricted" until you do. Use the legal name of the business from the start.

- Decide what counts as a result. A call, a form, a booking or an order. Then make sure it is counted, because a campaign without conversion tracking can only report clicks.

- Send each advert to a page that answers it. An advert for boiler repair should not land on a homepage about everything the company does.

- Keep the accounts in your own name. Google Ads, Analytics and the Business Profile should belong to the business, with access given to whoever helps you, so nothing is lost if that person changes.

## What to do today

- Claim and verify the Business Profile. Check the name, address, hours, phone number and categories.

- Write down the five searches a customer would type. Search them yourself and note who advertises and what they say.

- Pick one paid route from the table above. One, not three.

- Read your own adverts and landing page against the rules. Accurate, truthful, and nothing important left out. Remove any claim you cannot prove.

- Check the consent banner and the contact form. A clear cookie choice, and no pre-ticked box adding people to a mailing list.

- Set a budget you can leave running for a full month. A week is rarely enough to judge. If you would like a second pair of eyes on the plan first, that is what a PPC consultation is for, and Google Ads for small business sets out the options by budget.

- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/2567043?hl=en-GB
- https://support.google.com/localservices/answer/12174778?hl=en-GB&co=GENIE.CountryCode%3DGB

### FAQ

**How can I advertise my business for free in the UK?** Start with a Google Business Profile. Google says you can add or claim your business at no charge and manage how it shows up on Maps and Search. You need to verify the profile before you can edit it fully.

**What is the best way to advertise a small local business?** For a business people search for when they need it, a verified Business Profile and one Search campaign aimed at your area is the usual starting point. Trades and home services can add Local Services Ads, where you pay per lead after Google verifies the business.

**Who regulates advertising in the UK?** The Advertising Standards Authority enforces the advertising codes, and GOV.UK says adverts that break the rules may be withdrawn. Separate consumer law applies as well, with penalties of up to £300,000 or 10% of global turnover for enforcement action, according to GOV.UK.

**Do the advertising rules apply to my own website and my Google adverts?** Yes. The ASA's list of what it covers online includes claims made on a company's own website or app and paid-for search listings.

**Can I email people who have not asked to hear from me?** Not individuals. The ICO says you must not send marketing emails or texts to individuals without specific consent, with a limited exception for your own previous customers. Sole traders are treated as individuals. Corporate bodies can be emailed, and the ICO recommends keeping a list of those that object.
